--- title: "Plotting trajectories" --- The columns of a `(B, 157)` array are fortnightly windows spanning six years of simulation. Plot against time relative to the campaign. That puts the decision at zero and the response to its right. ## The setting The running example is a district with a measured under-5 prevalence of 0.45, pyrethroid resistance at 0.30, and pyrethroid-only nets at 70% coverage. The EIR comes from estiMINT. The net lethality comes from `calculate_dn0`. ::: {#941ad8f3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import calculate_dn0, load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model current = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=0.70) setting = pd.DataFrame([{ "prev_y9": 0.45, "dn0_use": current.dn0, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "itn_use": current.itn_use, "irs_use": 0.0, }]) eir = float(run_xgb_model(setting, load_xgb_model("prevalence"))[0]) print(f"dn0_use = {current.dn0:.3f}, itn_use = {current.itn_use}, eir = {eir:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dn0_use = 0.311, itn_use = 0.7, eir = 31.96 ``` ::: ::: The three candidate campaigns below are all at the same 70% coverage and differ only in the net product. Each restates `itn_future`. Leaving it at zero would withdraw the nets. ::: {#49ed8f1d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained( "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2", ) cases = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained( "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2", ) base = { "eir": eir, "dn0_use": current.dn0, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0, "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0, } products = { "pyrethroid-only": "py_only", "pyrethroid-PBO": "py_pbo", "pyrethroid-pyrrole": "py_pyrrole", } scenarios = [ dict(base, dn0_future=calculate_dn0(0.30, **{net: 0.70}).dn0, itn_future=0.70) for net in products.values() ] prev = prevalence.predict(scenarios) case = np.maximum(cases.predict(scenarios), 0.0) print(prev.shape, case.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (3, 157) (3, 157) ``` ::: ::: ## The time axis The axis is worth rebuilding from the checkpoint rather than from memory, since the three numbers that define it are sitting in the preprocessing config. ::: {#a53a3ec0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} cfg = prevalence.preprocessing_config abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(cfg["n_steps"]) years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365 idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]))) ``` ::: ## The figure ::: {#a9aa5301 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax_p, ax_c) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.2, 6.4), sharex=True) for label, p, c in zip(products, prev, case): ax_p.plot(years, p, label=label) ax_c.plot(years, c, label=label) for ax in (ax_p, ax_c): ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax_p.set_ylabel("Prevalence") ax_p.set_title("Parasite prevalence") ax_p.legend(loc="lower right") ax_c.set_ylabel("Cases per 14-day window") ax_c.set_xlabel("Years relative to the campaign") ax_c.set_title("Clinical cases") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Prevalence and clinical cases under three net products, all at 70% coverage, in a district with pyrethroid resistance of 0.30. The dashed rule marks the campaign.](plotting_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two stacked panels sharing a time axis running from three years before the campaign to three years after. The upper panel shows prevalence, the lower panel clinical cases. The three products separate only after the campaign, with pyrrole lowest, then PBO, then pyrethroid-only.'} ::: ::: ## Reading it The three curves lie exactly on top of one another to the left of the rule, and separate only to the right of it. The campaign covariates are masked before day 3285, so three scenarios that differ only in their campaign share an identical pre-campaign history. If your pre-campaign curves *do* separate, you have changed something in the present (`dn0_use`, `itn_use`, `irs_use` or the EIR) when you meant to change only the campaign. The baseline is not flat, because `model_start_day` is day 2190 and the campaign is day 3285, exactly 1095 days or three years apart. The window opens on the previous mass distribution and closes on the next one. Prevalence falls through the first year as those nets take effect, then rises for two more as they wear out and are not replaced, arriving at the campaign at its highest point in the cycle. The same three-year saw-tooth repeats after the campaign, on the right-hand half of the figure. ::: {#c8c5acf1 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pre = prev[:, :idx_y9 + 1] annual = {a: float(prev[0][(years >= a) & (years < a + 1)].mean()) for a in range(-3, 3)} print("prevalence given to estiMINT :", 0.45) print(f"emulator at the campaign : {prev[0, idx_y9]:.3f}") print() print(f"pre-campaign range : {pre.min():.3f} to {pre.max():.3f}") print(f"campaigns identical before 0 : {bool(np.allclose(pre[0], pre[1]) and np.allclose(pre[1], pre[2]))}") print() for a, mean in annual.items(): print(f"mean prevalence, year {a:+d} : {mean:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` prevalence given to estiMINT : 0.45 emulator at the campaign : 0.456 pre-campaign range : 0.288 to 0.491 campaigns identical before 0 : True mean prevalence, year -3 : 0.332 mean prevalence, year -2 : 0.369 mean prevalence, year -1 : 0.455 mean prevalence, year +0 : 0.339 mean prevalence, year +1 : 0.402 mean prevalence, year +2 : 0.490 ``` ::: ::: That output contains two checks, since the pre-campaign years are identical across the three campaigns, as the masking requires, and at the campaign step the trajectory passes within a few thousandths of 0.45, the prevalence estiMINT was given. Run that round trip, prevalence to EIR to trajectory, on every scenario. It costs one line. The agreement holds *at `idx_y9`* and not on average, because the annual means run from 0.33 to 0.46 across the baseline, so a scenario judged by its mean baseline prevalence will appear badly wrong when it is not. `prev_y9` is a point on the trajectory, and `idx_y9` is where to read it. A trajectory that misses your measured prevalence at that step means something is wrong upstream, most often in `dn0_use` or `itn_use`. Three years on, the ranking is the one the `dn0` table predicts, with pyrrole below PBO below pyrethroid-only. The gaps are modest at 30% resistance and 70% coverage. They are the basis of the procurement decision. ::: {#e1ed8841 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} for label, p, c in zip(products, prev, case): print(f"{label:20s} prevalence {p[-1]:.3f} cases {c[-1]:6.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pyrethroid-only prevalence 0.484 cases 2.43 pyrethroid-PBO prevalence 0.470 cases 2.41 pyrethroid-pyrrole prevalence 0.464 cases 2.39 ``` ::: ::: ## A tidy frame Two arrays and an axis are enough for matplotlib, while anything else (a `ggplot`-shaped workflow, a `groupby`, a CSV for a collaborator) wants the data long, one row per scenario per timestep. ::: {#ded7923d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} tidy = pd.DataFrame({ "net": np.repeat(list(products), len(years)), "years": np.tile(years, len(products)), "abs_day": np.tile(abs_t, len(products)), "prevalence": prev.ravel().astype(float), "cases": case.ravel().astype(float), }) print(tidy.shape) tidy.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (471, 5) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
net years abs_day prevalence cases
0 pyrethroid-only -3.000000 2190 0.449371 2.086377
1 pyrethroid-only -2.961644 2204 0.450827 1.185663
2 pyrethroid-only -2.923288 2218 0.438303 0.658037
3 pyrethroid-only -2.884932 2232 0.415712 0.613480
4 pyrethroid-only -2.846575 2246 0.393178 0.564645
``` ::: ::: `prev.ravel()` flattens row by row, which is the order `np.repeat` lays the labels out in. The result is three blocks of 157 rows, one block per scenario. The `astype(float)` widens the emulator's `float32` output to double, which stops rounding from producing things like `274.299988`. From here `tidy.to_csv("trajectories.csv", index=False)` writes a file anyone can open in R. A `groupby` gives the case burden of each campaign. ::: {#afd406d0 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} post = tidy[tidy["years"] >= 0] post.groupby("net", sort=False)["cases"].sum().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` net pyrethroid-only 146.6 pyrethroid-PBO 125.6 pyrethroid-pyrrole 118.7 Name: cases, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Filter to `years >= 0` before totalling anything you intend to compare. Summing over all 157 windows adds the same three baseline years to every product. The absolute differences survive that, since the baseline is shared, but every total is inflated by the same constant, so any proportion computed from them (cases averted, relative reduction) understates the campaign. ## Next - [Performance and caching](performance.qmd) — running many of these at once. - [Comparing campaigns](../06-scenarios/comparing.qmd) — the same comparison through the pipeline.
